description_full: General Motors Company designs, builds, and sells trucks, crossovers, cars, and automobile parts worldwide. It operates through GM North America, GM International, and GM Financial segments. The company markets its vehicles primarily under the Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC, Baojun, and Wuling brand names. In addition, it sells trucks, crossovers, cars, and automobile parts through retail dealers, distributors and dealers, as well as to fleet customers, including daily rental car companies, commercial fleet customers, leasing companies, and governments. Further, the company offers various range of after-sale services through dealer network, such as maintenance, light repairs, collision repairs, vehicle accessories, and extended service warranties. Additionally, it provides automotive financing; and software-enabled services and subscriptions. General Motors Company was founded in 1908 and is based in Detroit, Michigan.

financial_summary: General Motors Company is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $72.5B market cap on $185.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 24% against a 10% cost of capital — a 14-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $17.6B in free cash flow — roughly 9 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 9.96× so those profits are backed by real cash.

On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and thin 0.4× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 9.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.2× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.2) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Recent layoff news — often the market’s first signal that growth is under pressure or costs are being rebased
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment
Minimal goodwill on the balance sheet — low impairment risk
Consumer Cyclical sector outperforming the broader market over the past quarter
